Vidhana Soudha.script: As you begin your drive out of central Bengaluru, you're passing Vidhana Soudha, the seat of Karnataka's Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council. The building was completed in 1956, and its design is a striking blend of Neo-Dravidian and Indo-Saracenic styles, drawing on several Indian architectural traditions. Look up at the central dome: it is crowned by a likeness of India's State Emblem. The building was imagined by Chief Minister Kengal Hanumanthaiah as a "people's palace," representing democratic government rather than royal authority. Its foundation stone was laid by India's first Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, on 13 July 1951. Construction involved more than 5,000 workers, including some prisoners who were released after completing the work. There was also controversy around the project. Opposition leaders accused the government of excessive spending, and an Inquiry Committee was appointed to examine those claims. One detail you can spot on the building is the inscription, "Government Work is God's Work." So as you leave Bengaluru behind, you're starting your journey beside one of the state's most important symbols of democratic government.

Attara Kacheri.script: As you begin your drive through central Bengaluru, you’re passing Attara Kacheri, the red-painted building opposite Vidhana Soudha. Today, it is the principal bench of the Karnataka High Court, but its story began as a government office building. Construction started in October 1864 and was completed in April 1868. It brought the administrative departments of the princely state of Mysore under one roof. The name Attara Kacheri means “eighteen departments,” referring to the way the Mysore government was reorganised after an embassy to Aurangzeb’s court in 1699. There’s also a darker chapter. After a revolt in the Kingdom of Mysore in 1830, the British East India Company took administrative powers from the Wadiyar in 1831 and placed the government under a British Commission. Decades later, Attara Kacheri itself nearly disappeared. In 1982, the Karnataka government approved its demolition. A legal challenge followed, and after the Supreme Court asked the state to reconsider, the demolition proposal was dropped in 1985. So as you continue past it, you’re seeing a building that survived not just changing governments, but a serious attempt to erase it.

Cubbon Park.script: As you drive through central Bengaluru, you’re approaching Cubbon Park, officially called Sri Chamarajendra Park. It began in 1870 under Major General Richard Sankey, covering 100 acres. Today, the park is reported to cover about 300 acres. Its history is also a story of changing names. It was first called Meade’s Park, then became Cubbon Park in 1873 after Sir Mark Cubbon. In 1927, it was renamed Sri Chamarajendra Park to commemorate the Silver Jubilee of Sri Krishnaraja Wodeyar’s rule. Look around, and you’ll see how the park blends trees, rock outcrops, lawns, flowerbeds, buildings, and monuments. There’s also a surprising link to the city’s colonial past: before India’s Independence, the British Royal Air Force played western band music here every Saturday evening. The park even connects with the Attara Kacheri you’ve just heard about, with its formal gardens extending from that historic building toward the museum. So as you pass by, you’re not just seeing greenery in the middle of Bengaluru—you’re passing through a place shaped by more than a century and a half of changing names, landscapes, and history.

M G Road, Bengaluru.script: You’re now passing along M G Road, running from Trinity Circle to Anil Kumble Circle. Before independence, it was known as South Parade. On 26 February 1948, it was renamed Mahatma Gandhi Road. Today, it’s one of Bengaluru’s busiest roads, lined with shops, restaurants, offices and theatres. Its Metro line connects the city’s east and west.

Lal Bagh.script:
As you drive through south Bengaluru, you're passing close to Lalbagh, one of the city's historic green spaces. Its story begins in 1760, when King Hyder Ali commissioned the garden during the Sultanate of Mysore. His son, King Tipu Sultan, completed it and added to its collection of trees and plants by bringing them in from several countries.

The name Lalbagh is interesting in itself. A Bagh means garden in Hindustani, while the meaning of Lal is debated. It could refer to the colour red, because of the garden's original floral composition, or it could mean beloved. The garden was designed along the lines of Mughal Gardens, including those that once stood at Sira, 120 kilometres from Bengaluru.

Over time, Lalbagh became much more than a royal garden. After the British conquest of the Kingdom of Mysore in 1799, it passed through several forms of British and government management. In 1856, it was made the Government Botanical Garden. Its purpose included improving the use of indigenous plants, introducing useful exotic species, and exchanging plants and seeds with other gardens.

That botanical role left a remarkable legacy. The garden's collections included plants such as coffee, tea, macadamia nuts, rhododendrons, camellias and bougainvilleas. Plants also arrived from places including Persia, Afghanistan and France. Today, Lalbagh covers 240 acres and has more than 1,000 species of plants, including many trees that are more than a hundred years old.

And then there's the Glass House. Its foundation stone was laid on 30 November 1889, and the building was completed in 1890-91. It was modeled on London's Crystal Palace and became a venue for flower shows. Today, Lalbagh holds two major flower shows, around Republic Day and Independence Day.

There is also a darker chapter in its history. Lalbagh once had a menagerie and an aviary. A 1914 report described tigers, a rhinoceros, an orangutan, several kinds of deer, emus, bears and peacocks. After the plague, maintenance deteriorated, and there were proposals to close the menagerie and aviary.

So as you continue toward Mysuru, Lalbagh is more than a park beside the road. It is a place where royal ambition, botanical experimentation, British administration and Bengaluru's modern public life all meet.
Lal Bagh.more_script:
If you want one detail that really puts Lalbagh's age into perspective, look toward the Lalbagh Rock. The garden adjoins a large rock with a tower associated with Kempegowda, the founder of Bengaluru. The rock itself is described as dating back 3,000 million years.

The garden also changed considerably under its superintendents. John Cameron, who came from Kew, helped introduce plants including Araucarias, cypresses and topiaries. He also supported the introduction of commercial crops such as cabbage, cauliflower, turnip, radish, rhubarb, celery and kohlrabi. Trees introduced during this period included the baobab from Africa, Brownea rosea from the Caribbean, and Catha edulis from Yemen.

The Glass House became one of Lalbagh's defining structures. It was built with iron pillars cast by Walter Macfarlane and Company of Glasgow. The structure was later extended in 1935 using steel from the Mysore Iron and Steel Company at Bhadravathi.

Lalbagh's history also includes periods when public life was interrupted. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the garden closed on 21 March 2020 to avoid public gatherings. The Independence Day flower show that year was cancelled, and the mango and jackfruit melas were not held.

Today, the garden remains a major urban green space, with lawns, flowerbeds, lotus pools, fountains and an intricate irrigation system. Its long history is still visible in its old trees, plant collections, Glass House and ancient rock.

Ramanagara.script: You’re approaching Ramanagara, about 50 kilometres from Bengaluru. Look toward the surrounding hills, now called the Ramagiri hills. They’re also known by a much more familiar nickname: the Sholay hills. That name comes from the 1975 Bollywood film Sholay, which was shot here. More recently, the hills also featured in the 2022 Malayalam film Jana Gana Mana. But Ramanagara is more than a film location. It is known for sericulture and is nicknamed Silk Town and Silk City. The silk produced here becomes an input for famous Mysore Silk, and Ramanagara is described as the largest market for silk cocoons in Asia, with about 50 tonnes arriving each day. There’s an older layer to the town’s story too. During the rule of Tipu Sultan, it was known as Shamsherabad or Ramserpuram. Later, in pre-independence times, it was called Closepet, a name still retained in geology through the Closepet granites. As you pass, those hills carry both cinematic history and a much older geological story.

Kaveri.script: You’re crossing the Kaveri River now, near Srirangapatna. This is one of southern India’s major rivers, flowing for roughly 800 kilometres from its source in Karnataka to the Bay of Bengal. Here, the river does something striking: it forms the river island of Srirangapatna before widening and continuing eastward. The Kaveri has supported agriculture in this region for centuries, helping sustain early agricultural states including the Chola and Pandya kingdoms. Its importance is still very much alive today. Multiple dams and reservoirs along the river support irrigation and hydroelectric power, while its waters remain the subject of a long-standing dispute between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. There’s also a cultural side to the river. In Hinduism, the Kaveri is revered as one of the seven sacred rivers and is personified as the goddess Kaveriamma. But the river also faces environmental pressure. Dams and flow regulation have disrupted aquatic habitats and fish migration, while reduced natural flows have contributed to declines in migratory fish populations. As you cross, you’re passing over a river that has shaped both human life and the landscape around it.

Srirangapatna.script:
You’re approaching Srirangapatna, a town on an island formed by the Kaveri River. The river surrounds the town, with its main channel on the eastern side and the Paschima Vaahini, a branch of the same river, on the west. So as you pass through, you’re entering a place where the river itself is part of the story.

Srirangapatna gets its name from the Ranganathaswamy Temple, which was consecrated around 984 CE. The temple is dedicated to Ranganatha, a manifestation of Vishnu, and the town became one of the important Vaishnavite pilgrimage centres of South India. The temple was built by rulers of the Western Ganga dynasty in the 9th century and later strengthened and improved architecturally. Its design brings together Hoysala and Vijayanagar styles.

But Srirangapatna is just as important for its political and military history. During the Vijayanagara Empire, it became the seat of a major viceroyalty. In 1610, Raja Wodeyar I defeated Rangaraya, the viceroy of Srirangapatna, and celebrated the Navaratri festival there. Over time, control of the town and its fort came to represent sovereignty over the Kingdom of Mysore.

Later, Srirangapatna became the capital of Mysore under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan. Its history also has a darker side. During Tipu Sultan’s wars, entire communities including Nairs, Kodavas and Mangalorean Catholics were deported to Srirangapatna from conquered regions and held in bondage until their freedom followed Tipu’s defeat in 1799.

The town then became the setting for the decisive battle of the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War in 1799. Tipu Sultan was killed within the fort. The victorious forces plundered Srirangapatna and ransacked Tipu’s palace. Yet parts of the battlefield remain, including the ramparts, the Water Gate and the area where British prisoners were held.

Today, the monuments of this island town have been nominated for UNESCO World Heritage status, with the application pending on the tentative list. As you pass Srirangapatna, you’re passing through a place where religion, the Kaveri, royal power and war all meet.
Srirangapatna.more_script:
If you want to look a little deeper, Srirangapatna’s fort was more than a monument. Because it was the fortification nearest to Mysore’s capital, it became the last bastion and defence of the Kingdom of Mysore in case of invasion.

The town was also the setting for an important political settlement. On 18 March 1792, the Treaty of Seringapatam was signed, ending the Third Anglo-Mysore War. Its signatories included Lord Cornwallis on behalf of the British East India Company, representatives of the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Maratha Empire, and Tipu Sultan, the ruler of Mysore.

Seven years later, the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War reached its decisive moment here. A combined force of 50,000 men, provided equally by the Nizam of Hyderabad and the East India Company and commanded overall by General George Harris, fought Tipu Sultan’s forces. Tipu was killed within the fort, and the victorious army plundered the town and ransacked his palace.

The aftermath reached far beyond Srirangapatna. Among the valuables taken to England were Tipu Sultan’s clothing, shoes, sword and firearms. Tipu’s Tiger, an automaton depicting a tiger attacking a British soldier, is held by the Victoria and Albert Museum.

And there is another layer to the town: pilgrimage. The Ranganathaswamy Temple is known as Adi Ranga, the first of three Ranganatha temples situated on natural islands in the Kaveri. The other two are Madhya Ranga at Shivanasamudra and Antya Ranga at Srirangam. Tradition holds that the islands formed in the Kaveri are consecrated to Sri Ranganathaswamy.

Mysore Palace.script:
As you arrive in Mysuru, you're approaching Mysore Palace, also known as Amba Vilas Palace. This is more than a royal residence. It was the official home of the Wadiyar dynasty and the seat of the Kingdom of Mysore.

The story of this site goes back centuries. A fort with earthen walls was constructed here in 1524 by Chamaraja Wodeyar III. The first recorded mention of a palace comes from 1638, when Kanthirava Narasaraja I rebuilt it after it was destroyed by a lightning strike. Over the years, the palace was destroyed and rebuilt several times.

Then came a major turning point. In 1793, Tipu Sultan demolished the palace and parts of the fort's outer walls, using their materials to begin a new fortress called Nazarabad. After Tipu's death at the Battle of Srirangapatna in 1799, the British installed five-year-old Krishnaraja Wodeyar III on the throne and rebuilt the palace. That restored palace was mainly wooden and built in a Hindu architectural style.

But the palace you see today came after another disaster. On February 20th, 1897, a ruinous fire destroyed much of the northern portion of the building. Eight people died. The fire destroyed one-fifth of the palace, including the durbar hall, armory, Sanskrit library, and music room. The royal family moved to nearby Jaganmohan Palace while a new structure was commissioned.

Construction of the present palace began in 1897 and finished in 1912. Its design is attributed to British architects Henry Irwin and E.W. Fritchley, and the building combines Indo-Islamic, Rajput, Hoysala, and Gothic styles.

There's another surprising connection to the journey you've just made. The palace was rebuilt after Tipu Sultan's death at Srirangapatna, a place we already passed on this trip.

Today, the palace contains a public museum and the living quarters of Yaduveer Krishnadatta Chamaraja Wadiyar, the current ceremonial head of the Wadiyar dynasty. Its grounds also contain gardens, Hindu temples, and the old fort walls. And since the early nineteenth century, Mysore Dasara has been held on these grounds, ending with an elephant procession on Vijayadashami.

So as you pass through Mysuru, you're not just approaching a palace. You're approaching a place that has been rebuilt repeatedly, survived fire and political change, and remained at the center of Mysuru's royal history.
Mysore Palace.more_script:
If you want to look a little deeper, the palace's name itself has a story. Amba Vilas comes from Sanskrit. Ambā means "mother" and is an epithet for the Hindu goddess Durga. Local legend says Durga slew the demon king Mahishasura atop the nearby Chamundi Hills. Vilāsa refers to a residence of pleasure or luxury, a term commonly used for palaces in India during British rule.

The palace also played a surprisingly large role in the life of Mysuru. In 1805, Krishnaraja Wodeyar III held the first durbar, or royal assembly, there during Navaratri. By 1836, an estimated 6,000 soldiers, Brahmins, servants, and other workers were employed by the palace. By the time Krishnaraja died in 1868, that number was estimated at 10,000 people, roughly one out of every six residents in Mysuru.

The reconstruction after the 1897 fire was an enormous undertaking. The project was initially expected to cost Rs 25,00,000, but the estimated final cost rose to Rs 41,47,913. Government guidelines called for stone, brick, and iron to be used, while inflammable materials were kept to a minimum.

Scottish traveler William Murdoch visited in 1908, while construction was still underway. He described the intricate carvings of indigenous plants and animals in marble, granite, and teak, and noted that hundreds of carvers and thousands of masons were involved.

There is also a modern chapter to the story. In 1998, the Karnataka state government enacted the Mysore Palace Acquisition Act, acquiring ownership from the Wadiyar family. The act was challenged in court and remains the subject of an ongoing legal dispute.

As of 2024, more than four million people visit the palace each year. What began as a fortified royal site has become one of India's most famous tourist attractions.

Chamundi Hills.script: You’re in Mysuru now, and that hill rising ahead is Chamundi Hills. The hill reaches about 1,060 metres, and at its summit stands the Chamundeshwari Temple, which has been patronised for centuries by the rulers of Mysore. One of the most striking ways to reach the top is an ancient stone stairway of more than 1,008 steps, constructed in 1659 by Dodda Devaraja Wodeyar. About halfway up, you meet a huge Nandi carved from a single piece of black granite. It is 4.9 metres tall and 7.6 metres long. There’s also a story behind the city you’re driving through. Local legend says the goddess Chamundeswari killed the asura Mahishasura after a fierce battle. The old Kannada name Mahishooru literally means ‘the village of Mahishasura,’ giving the hill an indirect influence on the name Mysuru. But Chamundi Hills is more than a religious landmark. Its reserve forest supports remarkable biodiversity, including 193 recorded bird species and around 150 butterfly species. Its popularity also brings environmental pressure, especially plastic waste and stress on local ecosystems. So as you pass beneath the hill, you’re looking at a place where legend, pilgrimage, the city’s name, and a living ecosystem all meet.
